difficultyReason: The flaw is a classic necessary/sufficient confusion — a condition stated as necessary is treated as sufficient in the conclusion. Two answer choices have surface plausibility by sharing quantifier language, requiring the student to track the exact conditional reversal.
stimulus: Only researchers who have received institutional ethics board approval may conduct studies involving human subjects. Dr. Vasquez has received institutional ethics board approval. Therefore, Dr. Vasquez may conduct studies involving human subjects.
questionStem: The flawed reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to the flawed reasoning in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Only licensed electricians are permitted to install residential wiring in this city. Marchetti is a licensed electrician. Therefore, Marchetti is permitted to install residential wiring in this city.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Only registered voters are eligible to serve on a jury. Fontaine is eligible to serve on a jury. Therefore, Fontaine is a registered voter.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Only applicants with a graduate degree are considered for senior analyst positions. Huang has a graduate degree. Therefore, Huang will be hired as a senior analyst.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Only board-certified surgeons are allowed to perform this procedure. Dr. Okonkwo performed this procedure. Therefore, Dr. Okonkwo is a board-certified surgeon.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Only students who pass the qualifying exam advance to the dissertation stage. Reyes did not pass the qualifying exam. Therefore, Reyes will not advance to the dissertation stage.

explanations.correct: The stimulus treats ethics board approval as sufficient for being permitted to conduct human-subjects research, when the 'only' statement establishes it as merely necessary. C replicates this exactly: having a graduate degree is only a necessary condition for being considered, but the conclusion treats it as sufficient to guarantee being hired.
explanations.A: This is actually a valid inference. 'Only licensed electricians are permitted' means being licensed is necessary and (in this localized claim) the 'only' licenses permission, so having the license does permit the activity. No flaw is committed.
explanations.B: This commits the valid contrapositive reasoning: if only registered voters are eligible, then being eligible entails being registered. This is valid, not flawed — the direction of inference runs correctly from effect back to necessary condition.
explanations.C: Correct. Mirrors the stimulus precisely: 'only X are considered for Y' makes X a necessary condition for consideration, not a sufficient condition for being hired. Yet the conclusion treats having a degree as guaranteeing the job.
explanations.D: This is valid modus ponens on the contrapositive: performing the procedure entails being board-certified (since only board-certified surgeons may perform it). The inference runs in the correct direction with no flaw.
explanations.E: This is a valid inference by modus tollens: if passing is necessary to advance, then not passing entails not advancing. No flaw.

difficultyReason: The stimulus commits a correlation-to-causation flaw with a specific directional causal claim. Two trap answers also involve correlations but either reverse the causal direction or commit a different error, requiring students to match both the flaw type and its causal direction.
stimulus: A study of urban neighborhoods found that areas with more coffee shops also tend to have higher property values. Clearly, opening more coffee shops in a neighborhood causes property values to rise.
questionStem: Which one of the following arguments exhibits flawed reasoning most similar to that exhibited by the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Research shows that patients who take vitamin D supplements tend to have fewer depressive episodes. It must be that having fewer depressive episodes leads patients to take more vitamin D supplements.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Studies show that hospitals with more nurses per patient tend to have lower patient mortality rates. Therefore, the most effective way to reduce mortality is to eliminate unnecessary procedures.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Data show that students who eat breakfast regularly tend to earn higher grades. Therefore, eating breakfast regularly causes students to earn higher grades.

choices.label: D
choices.text: In regions where cycling is popular, residents tend to live longer. Clearly, the longer lifespan in these regions is due to the region's favorable geography, not cycling.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Companies that invest heavily in employee training consistently show higher profits. It follows that all companies that want higher profits should invest heavily in employee training, since this is the only proven path to profitability.

explanations.correct: The stimulus observes a correlation (more coffee shops, higher property values) and concludes that one factor directly causes the other, in that specific direction. C does exactly the same: correlation between breakfast-eating and grades is taken as proof that breakfast-eating causes higher grades, ignoring alternative explanations such as reverse causation or a third variable.
explanations.A: This commits a causal reversal — it acknowledges the same correlation but then flips the causal arrow from supplement→fewer episodes to fewer episodes→supplements. The flaw is reversed causal direction, not simple correlation-to-causation.
explanations.B: The conclusion introduces a completely unrelated remedy (eliminating procedures) that was never mentioned in the premise. This is a non sequitur or irrelevant conclusion, not a correlation-to-causation flaw.
explanations.C: Correct. Matches the stimulus flaw precisely: a correlation is presented, and a specific unidirectional causal claim is drawn without ruling out reverse causation or confounding variables.
explanations.D: This commits a different flaw: it acknowledges the correlation but then attributes the outcome to a third factor (geography) while dismissing the correlated variable. This is a competing-explanation move, not the same as inferring causation directly from correlation.
explanations.E: This goes further than mere correlation-to-causation by also adding an exclusivity claim ('the only proven path'). The flaw is compounded — it includes an unsupported 'only' assertion — making it a different, stronger error than the stimulus commits.

difficultyReason: The stimulus commits a part-to-whole (composition) fallacy — inferring that because every part of X has property P, X as a whole must have property P. Two answer choices involve similar compositional language but commit either the whole-to-part (division) error or a valid generalization, requiring students to carefully track the direction of inference.
stimulus: Each component of the new transit proposal — the expanded bus routes, the light-rail extension, and the revised fare structure — has been individually endorsed by city planners as cost-effective. Therefore, the transit proposal as a whole is cost-effective.
questionStem: The flawed reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to the flawed reasoning in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Every chapter of Serrano's novel has been praised by reviewers as gripping and well-paced. Therefore, Serrano's novel as a whole is likely to be gripping and well-paced.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The investment portfolio as a whole has yielded strong returns this quarter. Therefore, each individual asset in the portfolio must have yielded strong returns this quarter.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Several of the ingredients in this dish are, on their own, quite bitter. Therefore, at least some bitterness can be detected in the dish as a whole.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Most economists agree that reducing trade barriers promotes growth. Since the proposed treaty reduces trade barriers, it will likely promote growth.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Every brick in this wall is lightweight. Therefore, the wall itself is lightweight.

explanations.correct: The stimulus infers that because each part has property P (cost-effective), the whole must have property P. This is the composition fallacy. E replicates this exactly: each individual brick is lightweight, therefore the entire wall (composed of many bricks) is lightweight — a clear composition fallacy, since aggregate weight can differ fundamentally from individual component weight.
explanations.A: This is a superficially tempting answer because it moves from parts (chapters) to whole (novel). However, properties like 'gripping' and 'well-paced' are plausibly preserved across the whole when every part has them — this is closer to a valid inference. More importantly, it lacks the clear quantitative mismatch that makes composition a fallacy. It does not match the flaw as precisely as E.
explanations.B: This commits the opposite error: division fallacy — inferring from a property of the whole to a property of each part. The direction of inference is reversed relative to the stimulus.
explanations.C: This is actually a valid (or near-valid) inference: if several components are bitter, detecting some bitterness in the whole is a reasonable, cautious conclusion. The conclusion is hedged ('at least some') and does not overstate, so no composition fallacy is committed.
explanations.D: This is a straightforward deductive application of a general principle to a specific case (modus ponens structure). No part-to-whole reasoning is involved; this argument is valid.
explanations.E: Correct. Each part (brick) has property P (lightweight); conclusion: the whole (wall) has property P (lightweight). This is the composition fallacy in its clearest form, directly mirroring the stimulus.
